Nutrition Guidelines for Post-Surgical Recovery

Proper nutrition plays a critical role in wound healing, immune function, and overall recovery after surgery. This document provides general dietary guidance for patients recovering from orthopedic procedures.

Caloric and Protein Requirements:
After surgery, your body requires increased calories and protein to support tissue repair. Aim for a well-balanced diet providing adequate calories to support your activity level. Protein is especially important — target at least 1.2–1.5 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day during the first 8 weeks of recovery. Good protein sources include lean meats (chicken, turkey, fish), eggs, dairy products (milk, yogurt, cheese), legumes (beans, lentils), and nuts and seeds.

Vitamin and Mineral Support:
Several nutrients are particularly important for surgical recovery:

Vitamin C: Essential for collagen synthesis and wound healing. Found in citrus fruits, bell peppers, strawberries, and broccoli. Aim for at least 75–90 mg per day from food sources; your provider may recommend a supplement.

Vitamin D and Calcium: Important for bone health, particularly after joint replacement. Dairy products, fortified foods, fatty fish, and leafy greens provide calcium. Vitamin D is found in fatty fish and fortified dairy; sun exposure also stimulates production. Discuss supplementation with your physician.

Zinc: Supports immune function and wound healing. Found in meat, shellfish, legumes, and whole grains.

Iron: Important if you lost blood during or after surgery. Red meat, spinach, fortified cereals, and legumes are good sources. If your physician recommends an iron supplement, take it with vitamin C to improve absorption.

Vitamin K and Warfarin:
If you are taking warfarin (Coumadin) as a blood thinner, maintaining a consistent level of vitamin K in your diet is important, as vitamin K affects how warfarin works. Do not drastically increase or decrease your intake of vitamin K-rich foods. Vitamin K is found in leafy green vegetables (spinach, kale, broccoli, Brussels sprouts). You do not need to eliminate these healthy foods, but keep your intake consistent from week to week. Inform your anticoagulation team of any major dietary changes.

Hydration:
Adequate fluid intake supports circulation, kidney function, medication processing, and overall healing. Aim for at least 8 glasses (64 oz) of water per day unless your physician has recommended fluid restrictions. Limit caffeinated and sugary beverages, which can contribute to dehydration. Signs of dehydration include dark urine, dry mouth, dizziness, and headache.

Foods to Avoid or Limit During Recovery:
- Alcohol: Avoid alcohol entirely if you are taking opioid pain medications, blood thinners, or antibiotics, as alcohol interacts with these medications and impairs healing.
- High-sodium foods: Excess sodium promotes water retention and swelling. Limit processed foods, canned soups, and fast food.
- High-sugar foods: Excess sugar can impair immune function and promote inflammation. Limit sweets, sugary drinks, and refined carbohydrates.
- Grapefruit and grapefruit juice: Grapefruit can interact with certain medications including some cholesterol-lowering drugs and immunosuppressants. Check with your pharmacist.

Nutrition and Wound Healing:
Malnutrition significantly impairs wound healing and increases the risk of surgical site infections. If you have difficulty eating due to nausea, poor appetite, or difficulty preparing meals, contact your care team. Your case manager can connect you with nutritional support services, meal delivery programs, or a registered dietitian consultation if needed.

Supplements:
Do not start new supplements without consulting your physician, as some supplements (including vitamin E, fish oil, garlic, ginkgo, and others) can affect bleeding time and interact with warfarin or other medications you may be taking.
